clue.text: Elevated uncertainty reported in thieves' den?

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so what counts is how the words sound when spoken

parts.note: elevated is high and uncertainty is doubt; said quickly the two words run together

explanation.surface: Mysterious rumours of something lofty are said to be circulating inside a gang of thieves' lair.
explanation.walkthrough: HIGH DOUBT said aloud runs together into HIDEOUT; the question mark admits the definition is a little loose.
explanation.definitionFit: A hideout is a secret place where criminals lie low, such as a robbers' lair or gang's retreat.

clue.text: Difficult to hide old collection

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it tucked away inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: difficult means hard
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: It is hard to conceal an ancient set of belongings.
explanation.walkthrough: The first word hides the second: the abbreviation for old goes inside a word meaning difficult.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoard is a stored-up stock of money or valuables, a kind of accumulated stash or collection.

clue.text: Author Margaret to become wet maybe

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the English novelist, author of The Millstone
second meaning: an old verb for getting wet and muddy by trailing through dirt

explanation.surface: A novelist is destined to be drenched, or perhaps to turn feeble and wishy-washy.
explanation.walkthrough: Margaret Drabble is an English novelist; the verb drabble, to get draggled and wet in mud, is rare, hence 'maybe'.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of novelist Margaret Drabble is also a dialect verb meaning to get wet and muddy by trailing.

clue.text: Kitchen item found in Coventry

indicators.note: something found in a place is lying within it, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the second to fifth letters of the city name

explanation.surface: A piece of kitchen equipment was discovered in the English city of Coventry.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer sits inside the city name, letters two to five.
explanation.definitionFit: An oven is a standard cooking appliance, the sort of equipment every kitchen contains.

clue.text: There is no seaside fog? This may suggest you can come out now

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: the shoreline can be seen plainly with no mist

definitions.text: This may suggest you can come out now
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the idiom telling someone hiding that nobody is watching

explanation.surface: A weather observation about a misty shore, followed by a whispered all-clear to someone in hiding.
explanation.walkthrough: The first half takes the idiom literally; the question mark flags that playful literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is said to someone hiding or sneaking about, meaning nobody is watching and it is safe to emerge.

clue.text: Little-known old boy's meeting French priest

parts.note: OB is old boy, a former pupil, plus the 'S
curé is the French word for a parish priest

explanation.surface: An obscure former pupil of a school gets together with a parish priest from France.
explanation.walkthrough: OB, old boy, is a British term for a former pupil of a school; the 's is kept as an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obscure is not widely known or recognised, so little-known is a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Very happy to be looking down on everyone?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the idiom for feeling elated
second meaning, read literally: perched at the summit of the globe, above all people

explanation.surface: Supreme contentment seems to go with a snooty habit of looking down on other people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Looking down on' suggests snobbery, but here it is physical: from the top of the globe everyone is below you.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone feeling elated and delighted, as if nothing could be better.

clue.text: Silly Soho chap about 51 who can't stop buying stuff

definitions.note: a relative clause standing for a noun: one who can't stop buying

indicators.note: about means around, so one set of letters goes around another
silly means foolish and muddled, so the letters get jumbled into nonsense order

parts.note: letters to rearrange
LI is 51 in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A foolish man from London's Soho district, around fifty-one years old, is a compulsive spender.
explanation.walkthrough: Soho is a lively shopping and entertainment district of central London, which suits the surface; its letters and CHAP are rearranged around the Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A shopaholic is a compulsive shopper, someone addicted to purchasing things they may not need.

clue.text: Lad spun around in elevated territory

indicators.note: turned around every which way, the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A boy twirled round and round on some high ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spun around' looks like one instruction, but 'spun' belongs to the letters and only 'around' does the shuffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Uplands are higher areas of a country, hilly or mountainous ground as opposed to lowlands.

clue.text: Keeps going and stops when impeded by river

indicators.note: something impeded has an obstruction lodged in its middle, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: stops means ends
the Ure is a river in Yorkshire, a crossword favourite

explanation.surface: A traveller carries on, halting only when a river blocks the way.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure is a river in North Yorkshire; it goes inside a word for stops.
explanation.definitionFit: To endure is to last or persist over time, so it means continuing or carrying on.

clue.text: Humiliation in a flat below stairs?

parts.note: taken as written
a basement flat lies below the stairs, beneath the ground floor

explanation.surface: Living in a servants' flat downstairs brings loss of dignity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Below stairs' is the old British term for the servants' quarters, so the surface suggests the shame of servitude.
explanation.definitionFit: Abasement is the act of lowering someone in dignity or esteem, which is what humiliation does.

clue.text: Tipsy getting round, I showed the way

parts.note: O is round in shape
taken as written
to lead is to show the way

explanation.surface: A slightly drunk person buying drinks for everyone boasts of leading the group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' suggests a round of drinks, which fits tipsy, but it is only the circle-shaped letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Oiled is informal slang for drunk, as in well-oiled, describing someone who has had a few drinks.

clue.text: What's owed girl? Respect ultimately

parts.note: a deb, short for debutante, is a young society girl

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: Asking what a young woman is due, and answering that in the end it is respect.
explanation.walkthrough: A deb is a debutante, a young upper-class woman making her formal entrance into society.
explanation.definitionFit: A debt is money or something else that one person is obliged to pay another.

clue.text: Company male, blunter grumbler

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for company
M is the abbreviation for male
plainer speaking is blunter

explanation.surface: A man at the firm, more outspoken than the rest, is always moaning.
explanation.walkthrough: The three pieces simply follow the clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: A complainer is someone who habitually moans and gripes, which is what a grumbler does.

clue.text: Damage made fence wobbly over time

indicators.note: in a down clue over means placed above, so one piece sits on top of the next
something wobbly is unsteady and out of true, so the letters are shaken into a new order

parts.note: letters to rearrange
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Harm has made a fence unsteady as the years went by.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down answer, 'over' means the rearranged letters stand above the abbreviation for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Defacement is the spoiling of a surface or appearance, a particular kind of harm or vandalism.

clue.text: At least fourteen in cathedral's evensong?

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the letters lie inside the run of words that follows

parts.note: runs from the possessive S through the start of the second word

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a cathedral's evening service draws a congregation of fourteen or more.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer straddles the apostrophe-S and the next word. Two sevens make fourteen, so a plural of seven means at least fourteen, which the question mark excuses.
explanation.definitionFit: Being a plural, the word needs two or more sevens, and two sevens add up to fourteen as a minimum.

clue.text: Female needs items mislaid — dental aids

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female
things mislaid are losses

explanation.surface: A woman has lost things and needs replacement toothcare supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash in the clue is punctuation only; 'needs' joins the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dental floss is thread used to clean between teeth, and the plural covers different kinds of it.

clue.text: Fellow at lunchtime possibly gets some bread

parts.note: a chap is a fellow
taken as written
one o'clock is a typical lunchtime, and 1 becomes the letter I

explanation.surface: A man picks up a loaf in his midday break.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'at lunchtime' as AT ONE; the digit 1 stands in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: A chapati is a flat unleavened bread from South Asian cooking, eaten with curry.

clue.text: Commanding Officer detaining fool in Italian town

indicators.note: to detain is to hold in custody, so one piece is held inside another

parts.note: CO is the abbreviation for Commanding Officer
an ass is a fool
taken as written

explanation.surface: An army commander locks up an idiot while stationed in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks like it links fool to the town, but it is part of what goes inside; the famous wartime battle of Monte Cassino suits the military surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassino is a town in central Italy below the monastery of Monte Cassino.

clue.text: A cricket club used to be under suspicion

parts.note: taken as written
CC is the abbreviation for cricket club
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sports club was once the subject of suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Used to be' reads as one phrase, but 'used' is a piece and 'to be' is the link.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone accused has been charged with wrongdoing, so they are suspected of an offence.

clue.text: Henry VIII's eminence

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for henry, the unit of inductance
VIII is 8 in Roman numerals, written out as a word

explanation.surface: The grandeur of King Henry VIII.
explanation.walkthrough: The king is split in two: his name gives an abbreviation and his numeral gives a number spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: An eminence is a piece of rising ground, so both words describe a lofty or elevated position.

clue.text: Pathetic pal she's ditched

indicators.note: something ditched has been crashed or wrecked, so the letters come out in a wrecked order

parts.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A sorry figure: the friend she has just dumped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditched' reads as dumped, but it is meant as crashed, as a pilot ditches a plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Hapless means unlucky and unfortunate, deserving of pity, which matches pathetic in its sense of pitiable.

clue.text: They are highly revered, any one of them being lower?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: ideas or institutions nobody dares criticise

definitions.text: any one of them being lower?
definitions.note: the plural answer is defined through a description of any one member
definitions.meaning: second meaning, read cryptically: a lower is something that lows, that is, moos

explanation.surface: Things held in great esteem, but any one of them might come down a peg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' looks like the opposite of high, but it is one that lows; a cow lows when it moos, and cows are held sacred in Hinduism.
explanation.definitionFit: Sacred cows are beliefs or institutions treated as beyond criticism, just as cattle are venerated in India.

clue.text: Bridge in Harrogate, say, given name

indicators.note: given here means with something added, so a further piece is attached after

parts.note: Harrogate is a spa town; 'say' shows it is only an example
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A bridge in the Yorkshire town of Harrogate has been given a name.
explanation.walkthrough: Harrogate is a Yorkshire town famous for its mineral springs, so it is an example of a spa.
explanation.definitionFit: A span is the stretch of a bridge between supports, and to span a gap is to bridge it.

clue.text: No 50s-style youth would be famous

parts.note: taken as written
a Ted, or Teddy boy, was a 1950s British youth in Edwardian-style drape jackets

explanation.surface: Claims that no young rebel of the fifties would ever become a celebrity.
explanation.walkthrough: Teddy boys were a British youth subculture of the 1950s, known for long jackets and quiffs.
explanation.definitionFit: Noted means well known or celebrated, so it is a direct synonym for famous or renowned.

clue.text: Fish hard for young mammal to swallow

indicators.note: to swallow is to take something inside, so one piece ends up within another

parts.note: a cub is the young of a bear, fox or lion
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A fish that is too tough for a young animal to gulp down.
explanation.walkthrough: The young animal takes in the pencil-grade abbreviation for hard.
explanation.definitionFit: The chub is a freshwater fish of the carp family found in European rivers.

clue.text: Children the item for discussion

definitions.meaning: first meaning: offspring, as in legal wording
second meaning: a topic or matter being debated

explanation.surface: The kids are the main topic on the meeting's agenda.
explanation.walkthrough: The legal sense of offspring, as in 'died without issue', is the less familiar meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both a person's offspring and a subject or point up for debate.

clue.text: New theatre is becoming most crude

indicators.note: something new has been remade, so the letters are formed afresh in another order

parts.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A modern playhouse is staging increasingly vulgar productions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' reads as describing a theatre, but it tells you to rearrange the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy humour is coarse and bawdy, so the superlative describes the most vulgar or unrefined.

clue.text: One getting on, sort led astray

indicators.note: going astray means wandering off course, so the letters drift out of their order

parts.note: letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An elderly person, the kind easily misled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting on' suggests boarding or getting along, but here it means ageing.
explanation.definitionFit: An oldster is an elderly person, and 'getting on' is the idiom for growing older.

clue.text: Corrupt activity involving arts graduates

indicators.note: to involve is to include or enclose, so one piece is wrapped round another

parts.note: a deed is an act or activity
BA is Bachelor of Arts, made plural

explanation.surface: Dodgy dealings implicating people with humanities degrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' looks like an adjective for the activity, but it is the definition, used as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Debased means morally degraded or lowered in quality, which matches corrupt in the sense of depraved.
